title: End-to-End latency profiling traces for serving runtime
content:
Summary

This document records our end-to-end latency profiling traces for the serving runtime. Goal: identify where p50/p95/p99 latency is coming from and produce concrete mitigations. Tests were run on the standard benchmark harness (see linked artifacts) against a 7B and 30B model variant to highlight behavior across model sizes.

Background and why this matters

Customer-facing SLAs require predictable p95 latency for short text completions. Recently we observed significant p99 tail spikes in production for several workloads. To prioritize work, we need an actionable per-stage breakdown showing which stages dominate different quantiles and which optimizations give the best ROI.

Testbed and configuration

- Hardware: 1x NVIDIA A100 80GB (prod-like), and a 1x T4 instance for low-cost comparisons.
- Model variants: 7B (float16), 30B (quantized int8 where applicable).
- Runtime: serving-runtime v2.14.0 with kernel selection enabled, batcher v1.9.
- Workloads: short-chat (prompt ~80 tokens) and long-completion (prompt ~400 tokens).
- Tracing: distributed traces collected via Jaeger, spans instrumented at these stages: ingress (HTTP + auth), request parse/route, batching queue, routing policy, preprocessor, model-inference (kernel), kv-cache lookup, postprocess/decoding, streaming/response flush, network egress.
- Sample size: 50k requests per workload per config; traces sampled at 10% for Jaeger (higher sampling for debug runs).

Methodology

- Compute p50/p95/p99 at end-to-end level and per span using histogram aggregation (HDR histograms).
- Also compute stage contribution to tail by measuring span duration percentiles and by bootstrapping to estimate per-stage additive effect on p99.
- Group traces by: warm vs cold (cold = model not warmed/start with empty KV cache), batch size (1 vs >1), and kv-cache hit/miss.
- Correlate with system metrics (GPU utilization, host CPU, IO wait) to validate hypotheses.

Key findings (short)

1) p50 is dominated by model-inference as expected, but p99 frequently dominated by batching queue jitter and kernel launch jitter for larger models.
2) KV-cache misses add a large variable penalty on p95/p99 for chat-like workloads (up to 120-250ms extra at p99 for 30B).
3) Cold-starts (cold model weights in GPU memory / cold CUDA context) cause a high p99 spike but are rare; pre-warm reduces this significantly.
4) Network/ingress is small overall, but spikes when many concurrent small requests cause socket contention on the host (observed p99 up to 40ms in one noisy host).

Representative numbers (short-chat workload, A100, 7B vs 30B)

- 7B baseline (batching disabled): end-to-end p50=45ms, p95=110ms, p99=210ms. Per-stage p99 breakdown (approx): ingress=5ms, parse/route=3ms, batching queue=15ms, routing policy=2ms, preproc=6ms, model-inference=150ms, kv-cache=10ms, postproc/decoding=12ms, streaming=7ms.

- 30B baseline (batching disabled): end-to-end p50=120ms, p95=300ms, p99=640ms. Per-stage p99 breakdown (approx): ingress=6ms, parse/route=4ms, batching queue=35ms, routing=3ms, preproc=10ms, model-inference=480ms, kv-cache=120ms, postproc=18ms, streaming=10ms.

- 30B with batching enabled (max_batch=8, dynamic batching): end-to-end p50=95ms, p95=260ms, p99=520ms. Note: batching reduced average latency and p95 slightly but introduced more variance at p99 due to queueing when single-request bursts occur.

Per-stage analysis and root causes

1) Model-inference span
- Dominant contributor to p50 and large contributor to tail. For the 30B model, p99 is ~3-4x p50. Causes: variable sequence length, kernel choice mismatch for some sequences, and occasional GPU scheduling latencies.
- Evidence: traces where model-inference span shows a bimodal distribution; lower mode corresponds to cached KV paths, upper mode to kernel-reconfigure path triggered by longer sequences.

2) Batching queue span
- Queueing accounts for up to 20-25% of p99 in scenarios with bursty arrivals. Dynamic batching helps throughput but increases tail when arrivals are sparse and we wait for batch fills.
- Evidence: scatter plots of batch size vs latency show small batches with long waits at p99.

3) KV-cache span
- Misses cause significant p95/p99 impact for chat workloads that reference different session histories. For 30B, an uncached KV lookup combined with decode overhead increased p99 by up to 250ms in some traces.
- Mitigation: increase cache prefetching for active sessions and adjust cache TTLs.

4) Kernel launch/recompile jitter
- Some traces show 50-120ms spikes due to GPU kernel warmup or fallback to slower kernels when heuristics choose suboptimal one. This is especially visible after model variants change or when sequence lengths exceed heuristics.

5) Cold-starts
- Cold CUDA context initialization and memory copies add up to 400-600ms for 30B in worst case. Pre-warm reduces tail by ~300ms.

6) Host-level contention
- CPU-side regex/postprocessing occasionally blocks when host CPU is saturated from background tasks; correlated to large context-switch rates.

Trace examples (high-level)

- Trace A (30B, p99=640ms): heavy contribution from model-inference (480ms) + kv-cache miss (120ms). Batching queue minimal.
- Trace B (30B, p99=520ms with batching): batching queue 110ms + model 300ms; shows waiting for batch fill then longer inference due to kernel fallback.

Recommendations and mitigations (prioritized)

1) Short term (low effort, high impact)
- Enable per-session KV prefetch for active chat sessions. Owner: Priya. Expected p99 reduction for chat workloads ~100-180ms.
- Add a lightweight warm-up hook for CUDA contexts on scale-up events. Owner: Diego. Expected p99 win ~200-300ms for cold cases.
- Add guardrails on dynamic batching: introduce a max-wait threshold for small requests to avoid long waits at p99. Owner: Runtime batcher team. Expected to reduce batching-induced tails.

2) Mid term (medium effort)
- Improve kernel selection heuristics by logging cases where fallback occurs and automatically surface candidates for kernel tuning. Owner: Serving runtime / kernel team.
- Implement async post-processing to move CPU-bound transforms off the critical path. Owner: Platform engineering.

3) Long term (higher effort)
- Investigate fused kernels or persistent CUDA contexts for large models to reduce kernel-launch overhead.
- Advance adaptive batching that considers request age and session hotness.

Action items and next steps

- PR#582: add KV prefetch hook for session reads (linked). Owner: Priya. ETA: 2 weeks.
- ENG-1245: batching max-wait threshold experiment in staging. Owner: Diego. ETA: 1 week for experiment, 3 weeks to roll.
- Observability: increase trace sampling for a 24h window for impacted regions to gather more p99 observations. Owner: Liam. ETA: 3 days.

Open questions

- How much tail is caused by multi-tenant host noise vs pure model/runtime issues? Need controlled single-tenant runs to isolate.
- What is the cost impact of pre-warming vs increased reserved capacity? Tradeoff analysis required.

Appendix: reproducibility notes

- Scripts used to produce the traces live in internal repo (see linked artifacts PR#582). Use benchmark harness with seed=42 and workload config file short-chat.json.
- To reproduce a p99 spike locally: run 30B with batching enabled, launch a burst of single-request arrivals with randomized inter-arrival times (0-20ms), and capture Jaeger traces at 100% sampling for the burst window.

Concluding remarks

This profiling run shows a mixed picture: model inference remains the dominant cost for median latency, but multiple smaller stages compound to form the p99 tail. Short-term wins around KV prefetch, CUDA warm-up, and batching thresholds are likely to yield measurable p99 improvements with modest implementation cost. The next step is to run the ENG-1245 batching experiment in staging and increase tracing coverage while we land the KV prefetch PR.
